header:
Date: 2026-03-04 | Start: 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Liam O'Reilly (Horizon Head of ML), Sofia Alvarez (Horizon CTO), Marcus Tan (Horizon Infra)
Meeting type: cost economics discovery (hosted vs dedicated vs private)
summary: Horizon Ventures is evaluating Redwood for a production LLM assistant used across several portfolio apps. Main focus on cost/unit economics: per-token pricing, batching and KV/prefix caching levers, and tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Customer provided rough scale targets and budget constraints; Redwood AE/SE explained pricing model, batching/caching impacts, and proposed benchmark + pricing spreadsheet to quantify savings. Action items agreed to share token histogram and run a benchmark on Redwood Dedicated test pool.
topics: Per-token pricing and unit economics (hosted vs dedicated)
Batching, KV/prefix caching, and quantization levers
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — quick intros. I'm Alex, AE at Redwood. Priya's our solutions engineer.
[00:08] Liam O'Reilly: Hey Alex, Liam here. We run inference infra for a few portfolio teams, so happy to dig in.
[00:13] Sofia Alvarez: Sofia, CTO at Horizon. Main ask: can you give us a sense of per-unit cost and how we control it across hosted/dedicated/private?
[00:22] Priya Rao: yeah absolutely. we'll cover high-level pricing then dig into batching, kv cache, quantization. just a heads up transcription might mangle some product names, but i'll try to be clear.
[00:31] Marcus Tan: quick context — our initial target is 5M tokens/day, peaks up to 12k qps short spikes, average prompt 220 tokens, response ~180 tokens. budget target is ~ $X per month — (Sofia: we'll share exact number after).
[00:46] Alex Kim: ok that's helpful. for hosted we price per token; for dedicated there's committed capacity + lower per-token unit economics, and private has higher fixed cost but gives you network isolation + KMS.
[00:58] Liam O'Reilly: can you put numbers around per-token? like hosted vs dedicated delta?
[01:03] Priya Rao: rough ballpark yes — hosted list price for our curated models starts at around $0.0004 per input token and $0.0006 per output token for the model class you're describing — again depends on model size. Dedicated effective per-token after commit can drop to ~30-50% of hosted rate when you amortize GPU cost over steady utilization. If you use caching/batching smartly it's even lower.
[01:29] Sofia Alvarez: Those ranges are useful; are those with or without the streaming overhead? we plan on streaming partial outputs to the client.
[01:36] Priya Rao: streaming itself is negligible on unit cost; main driver is total tokens generated + memory/KV cache behaviour. but note that continuous streams can keep KV cache warm which helps for follow-up tokens.
[01:48] Marcus Tan: you mentioned caching — what's the difference between prefix caching and kv cache in your platform? and how does it change cost?
[01:54] Priya Rao: great question. prefix caching stores common prompt prefixes on the server side so repeated contexts don't re-run the full attention; KV cache is per-session key-value acceleration for autoregressive decoding. in practice prefix caching helps reduce compute for repeat queries across users; KV cache reduces work on long sequences and for multi-turn. both reduce effective tokens processed on GPU cycles and thus lower per-token GPU time. we also do automatic prefix hashing to detect cache hits.
[02:18] Alex Kim: to make it concrete: if 30% of your traffic are repeat prefixes, we often see 15-30% cost reductions; if you have long multi-turn chat sessions, kv caching can cut on-device compute by 20-40% depending on sequence length. combined with batching you get multiplicative improvements across throughput.
[02:34] Liam O'Reilly: ok. batching — we have a latency SLO of 250ms P95 for interactive UI. does batching conflict with that?
[02:42] Priya Rao: batching is workload-aware. Redwood's runtime uses continuous batching with latency-aware windows; if you set a strict P95 SLO we will prioritize low-latency routes and dynamic batching windows shrink. so you still get batching benefits for background and lower-priority queries, but interactive paths use small batch sizes and shorter windows. the cost tradeoff is you pay a premium for lower tail latency — fewer tokens amortized per GPU cycle.
[03:05] Sofia Alvarez: so for our 250ms P95 — what's typical batching behavior and cost impact?
[03:10] Priya Rao: typically for 250ms P95 you might see 1.2–1.5x token cost vs fully batched throughput. if you relax to 500ms you often see a 30–40% drop in unit cost. these are heuristics; we'll quantify on your workload.
[03:24] Marcus Tan: we also care about quantization. does Redwood support 4-bit or 8-bit models and how does that feed into pricing?
[03:30] Priya Rao: we validate quantized variants; 8-bit is broadly supported and 4-bit can be used for compatible models. quantization reduces GPU memory and can increase throughput — that typically lowers effective per-token cost because you fit more batch in a GPU. pricing itself doesn't change linearly; the core delta comes from lower infra cost which we pass through in lower dedicated amortized rates.
[03:49] Liam O'Reilly: if we did a Dedicated commit, what's an example commit size versus our numbers? like how many GPUs, what kind of savings?
[03:57] Alex Kim: for 5M tokens/day with your token sizes you probably need a small dedicated pool — e.g., 1–2 A100-class GPUs with autoscaling to handle peaks. a 1-year commit that matches your baseline can cut per-token by ~40% compared to hosted list pricing. exact depends on utilization patterns; that's why we run a short benchmark.
[04:19] Sofia Alvarez: private deployment — we're especially interested in SOC2 / KMS. does private require on-prem hardware or can it be VPC-hosted?
[04:26] Priya Rao: both. private control plane with customer-managed VPC is common; on-prem is available for air-gapped environments. we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key management and provide audit logs. Private has higher fixed fees (licensing + infra) but gives you isolation and compliance guarantees.
[04:41] Marcus Tan: regarding benchmarking — what artifacts do you need from us to run a representative benchmark?
[04:46] Priya Rao: ideally a token histogram, sample prompts, daily qps profile (peak and baseline), and any special prompt templates that matter. we'll run the same prompt set against hosted and a dedicated test pool (same model variants + quantization) and share a spreadsheet with per-token breakdowns, latency percentiles, and cost estimates.
[05:02] Alex Kim: we'll also include sensitivity analysis: different batching window sizes, cache hit rates, and a few quantization configs.
[05:10] Liam O'Reilly: ok good. one of our concerns: do you provide pre-emptive scaling or will we need to handle spikes ourselves? if we hit 12k qps spikes how do you guarantee capacity?
[05:19] Priya Rao: for Hosted we have multi-tenant pools and regional fallback — but spikes can hit rate limits; we recommend burst protection + autoscaling policies on Dedicated. Dedicated has reserved capacity and burst to shared pools if allowed in the contract. we can set a policy to prioritize critical traffic.
[05:34] Sofia Alvarez: any gotchas on data retention or egress costs when running Dedicated vs Hosted?
[05:39] Alex Kim: hosted does ephemeral logs by default but you can opt into longer retention; audit logs are configurable. egress is typical cloud egress; Dedicated in customer VPC reduces egress if you keep traffic internal. we'll share our security/compliance deck.
[05:50] Marcus Tan: rough timeline — we want to decide in 3–4 weeks and start a pilot in April.
[05:56] Alex Kim: sounds feasible. next steps recap: we'll send pricing spreadsheet + sample ROI calc, Priya will run benchmark with your sample prompts, and Liam you'll share token histogram.
[06:05] Liam O'Reilly: yep i'll pull the data and send it.
[06:08] Sofia Alvarez: quick follow-ups on pricing — do you have minimum commit terms for Dedicated (months)?
[06:12] Alex Kim: typically 3/6/12 month commits; discounts scale with term. we can propose a short-term pilot commit for 3 months to validate economics.
[06:20] Marcus Tan: any internal tooling we need to adapt? like SDKs or routing config?
[06:24] Priya Rao: we have SDKs in python/node, and routing is controlled via a policy layer in the console (region, latency tier, fallback). for private deployments we do a one-time infra integration.
[06:33] Liam O'Reilly: one more question — how do you charge for tokenization differences? our prompts sometimes include emojis and non-english.
[06:39] Priya Rao: pricing is per model token as counted by our tokenizer. we can surface tokenization counts per sample in the benchmark and normalize costs. multilingual/emoji tokens typically slightly change counts but we show the normalized per-request delta in the report.
[06:52] Alex Kim: ok wrapping up — recap of next steps and action items, then we'll share the spreadsheet. thanks everyone.
[06:59] Sofia Alvarez: thanks, useful session.
[07:01] Marcus Tan: thanks all.
[07:03] (call ended)
